title: When Building Gets Easier, Designing Matters More
author: Darlene S. Range
summary: Reflecting on a graduate learning-design course, Range argues that as AI and authoring tools make building eLearning easier, the learning designer's value shifts to judgment. Her own difficulty was translating a mental picture into explicit specifications, which generative AI exposed by quickly producing the wrong thing from vague instructions. Designing a low-bandwidth, smartphone-first version taught her that accessibility, bandwidth and device are design decisions, not final technical checks. Vibe coding extended what she could build but could not decide how narration, branching and feedback should serve learners. She concludes the profession's worth lies in analyzing learners, choosing modality, designing assessment and taking responsibility for whether the product works. It is a personal reflection, so the evidence is her own project experience.
points: When AI builds quickly from instructions, unclear design specifications produce the wrong product just as quickly, so up-front specification matters more.
Accessibility, bandwidth and device size belong in the design stage; a course that works on the developer's computer proves nothing about the learner's environment.
AI can supply code and feedback text but cannot judge whether branching, assessment and narration choices serve the learner.
As producing artifacts gets easier, the learning designer's distinctive value is analysis, modality choice, assessment design and accountability for outcomes.
quotes: AI could produce something from my instructions very quickly, but if I had not clearly communicated what I was visualizing, it could also produce the wrong thing very quickly.

A course working on the computer where it was developed does not prove that it works for the learner. Accessibility, bandwidth, device size, navigation, and delivery are design decisions—not final-stage technical checks.
Code could make three branches work in any order. AI could generate feedback. Neither could independently determine whether those choices supported my learner or instructional purpose.

Even deployment required human oversight. Something as small as changing the index.html filename prevented my experience from behaving as expected. Vibe coding dramatically lowered the programming barrier, but it did not eliminate troubleshooting, testing, or responsibility for the finished product.

Someone can learn to operate Storyline. Someone can prompt AI to generate an HTML page. That does not mean that person knows how to analyze learners, recognize accessibility barriers, select an appropriate modality, create meaningful assessment and feedback, manage technological constraints, or recognize when a polished product is instructionally weak.

I can build something technically impressive and still make the wrong design decision. I can also build something lightweight, accessible, and relatively simple that serves the learner extremely well.
